title: Proposal and Scope of Work · Corbell Logistics
doc_title: Decisions that keep up with three sites
subtitle: A 12-week operating model project for Corbell Logistics

sections.title: Executive summary
sections.body:
Corbell Logistics has grown from one site to three in four years, and the way decisions get made has not kept up. On our call, Marcus put it simply: since Hillcrest opened, pricing and staffing questions wait for him, and the site managers wait with them.

This proposal sets out a 12-week operating model project to put those decisions with the people closest to the work, starting with a map of every decision at all three sites.

What it is costing today: overtime and missed delivery windows while approvals wait a day or more, in numbers [TO CONFIRM: last quarter's figures, which Nina is bringing]. What changes in the first 90 days: written decision rights at each site, a weekly review in place of daily approvals, and the new rules proven at Hillcrest before they reach the other two sites.

sections.title: Where you are today
sections.body:
- 140 people across three warehouses, with Hillcrest open since March 2026
- Pricing, staffing and escalation decisions still go to the COO
- The third site doubled the approvals that reach Marcus
- Site managers know what to do, but wait for a yes
- Nothing written down says who decides what at each site

sections.title: What we heard
sections.body:
**How decisions get made.** "Since Hillcrest opened, every pricing call comes to me," Marcus told us. A site manager can wait a day for an answer on a rate or a shift.

**What it costs today.** Overtime and late deliveries. Nina wants to see the cost in numbers before anything changes.

**What good looks like.** Site managers deciding pricing and staffing within clear limits, with Marcus reviewing once a week instead of approving every day.

**Who needs to be in the room.** Nina and the three site managers.

sections.title: Our recommendation
sections.body:
Write down who decides pricing, staffing and escalations at each site, and replace daily approvals with a weekly review. Try it at Hillcrest first, where the approvals doubled, then roll it out to the other two sites.

We will not reorganize teams or change systems in this project. The work is about who decides what, and how fast.

sections.title: Scope of work
sections.body:
- **Phase 1, Map (weeks 1 to 2):** we walk one week of approvals at each site. You share the approval log and make the site managers available. At the end you have a map of every decision and where it waits.
- **Phase 2, Design (weeks 3 to 6):** we draft decision rights with the site managers. Marcus and Nina review each draft. At the end you have written rules for pricing, staffing and escalations.
- **Phase 3, Pilot (weeks 7 to 10):** we run the rules at Hillcrest and meet weekly. The Hillcrest manager decides within the limits. At the end you have a tested version and a list of what had to change.
- **Phase 4, Roll out (weeks 11 to 12):** we bring the rules to the other two sites. The site managers train their leads. At the end you have one way of deciding across all three sites.
